chapters.name: Watching is not enough
chapters.note: I can see everything... but what actually matters?

props.label: what if this head were silent?

cap.1: You can already watch every step inside a model, but that only shows what happened. To learn what matters, change something mid-run and see what breaks.
cap.2: run_with_cache reads and stores every activation, but it cannot answer 'what if this head were silent?'. For that you need to write back into the forward pass.
cap.3: Observation gives correlation; causal claims need intervention. The cache is read-only, while a hook can replace an activation so every downstream computation uses the edited value.

cap.1: Picture the model as a conveyor belt with named windows. Station a worker at one: they note what goes past, or swap it, and the belt carries on with the swap.
cap.2: A hook is a function attached to a named activation. It receives (activation, hook); return nothing to just read, or return a tensor to replace it for everything downstream.
cap.3: TransformerLens puts a HookPoint (an identity nn.Module) at every named activation, so a hook binds to a tensor by name rather than to a layer, which is all PyTorch's own hooks can do.

cap.1: Your instructions are a list of pairs: which window, and which worker. Hand the list over and the model runs once with your workers in place.
cap.2: model.run_with_hooks(tokens, fwd_hooks=[(name, fn)]). The name can be a string, utils.get_act_name('z', layer), or a filter like lambda n: n.endswith('pattern').
cap.3: Names pick one activation; filters pick many. return_type='loss' measures the effect; None runs purely for side effects, such as a hook writing induction scores into an outer tensor.

chapters.name: Three jobs, one hook
chapters.title: every causal tool is a hook

cap.1: Almost every experiment later is just a different worker at a window: one empties the tray, one swaps in a tray from another run, one adds something.
cap.2: Ablation zeroes an activation, activation patching overwrites it from another run, steering adds a vector to it. Learn the hook API once and all three come free.
cap.3: Ablation, activation patching, path patching and steering vectors are all hook functions with different bodies; the experimental design lives in what you return, and where.

chapters.name: The leftover worker

left.title: reset_hooks() first
lines: the heads that matter stand out

chapters.verdict: Hooks are global model state. Reset before you measure.

cap.1: A worker from an earlier attempt is still at their window, quietly swapping trays. Now your 'normal' run is not normal, and every comparison comes out flat.
cap.2: If a hook raised an error, run_with_hooks never cleaned up, and add_hook persists by design. Call model.reset_hooks() before the clean baseline, every time.
cap.3: reset_hooks_end=True only runs if the pass completes. A stale ablation makes loss_no_ablation itself ablated, so the (n_layers, n_heads) scores are differences of two ablated runs.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Read with the cache, intervene with hooks

cap.1: Hooks turn watching into experimenting. Every 'does this part matter?' question later in the course is a hook doing a different job.
cap.2: Ablation, patching, steering, activation capping and probe interventions are all hooks. nnsight offers the same read-and-intervene idea with a different syntax.
cap.3: Hooks are the mechanism behind every causal claim in interpretability and every activation-level steering method: the lever that turns understanding a model into steering it.

coda.title: One window, four jobs: pick what the worker does

readouts.label: the worker's job
readouts.f: ['read only: nothing changes', 'ablate: set to zero', 'patch: value from another run', 'steer: add α × a vector'][job]

caption.1: Bars show what leaves the window. Switch jobs: reading changes nothing, zeroing empties it, patching swaps it, steering pushes it. Watch the score.
caption.2: Same hook point, four hook bodies. The score is what a later layer reads from this activation. Ablation removes this spot's contribution; patching imports the other run's; steering shifts it along a vector.
caption.3: Here the downstream readout is linear, so the effect of each intervention is its change in projection. Steering moves the score by α times the vector's projection (1.3 per unit α).

where_else: Ablation, activation patching and path patching: a hook that zeroes or swaps an activation
Steering vectors and activation capping: a hook that adds to or clamps the residual stream
Outside ML: debugger watchpoints and web middleware, code that intercepts a value at a named point

hamming.what: A function attached to a named activation inside a running model, which can read it or hand back a replacement.
hamming.when: Whenever you ask a model 'what if': ablate a head, patch in another run, add a steering vector, or record a statistic mid-run.
hamming.why: Watching only shows correlation; changing an activation mid-run and seeing what happens downstream is how you get causal evidence.

object.title: The belt of named windows
object.subtitle: A forward pass laid out as a conveyor, with a worker stationed at one window and a note-taker at another.

nodes.label: your hook: reads and hands back

cap.1: The forward pass as a belt of named windows, from tokens to logits.
cap.2: Every intermediate activation has a name, like blocks.0.attn.hook_z. Hooks attach to names, not to layers.
cap.3: HookPoints (identity modules) sit at every named activation, so you address tensors, not modules.

cap.1: A worker at hook_z reads each head's output and hands back an edited version. Everything after the window uses the edit.
cap.2: Returning a tensor replaces the activation for the rest of the forward pass. That is how ablation and patching work.
cap.3: A forward hook's return value substitutes the HookPoint's output, so all downstream computation is conditioned on the intervention.

cap.1: Below, the cache only copies what passes. It never sends anything back.
cap.2: run_with_cache is read-only: store and inspect. A hook can also write back and change what the model computes.
cap.3: Caching is observational, hooks are interventional; causal claims need the second.

cap.1: Leave a worker stationed and they keep editing every future run until you dismiss them.
cap.2: add_hook persists, and a crashed run skips cleanup. model.reset_hooks() dismisses every stationed worker.
cap.3: Hook registration is global model state: reset before every baseline so the 'clean' run really is clean.

predict.q: Your hook function returns nothing. What does the model use downstream?

options.t: The original activation, plus any in-place edits

predict.why: Returning None leaves the activation in place, so the hook only reads (or edits in place). Return a tensor to replace it.

predict.q: Your ablation sweep says no head matters: every score is about zero. What should you check first?

options.t: A stale hook left over from an earlier run
The model is too small to have important heads

predict.why: If a hook is still attached, the 'clean' baseline is already ablated, so every comparison comes out flat. Call model.reset_hooks() first.

object.where: Anywhere you instrument a running system at named points: debugger watchpoints, network taps, web middleware.
